documents.title: Endocrinology Follow-up
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
OUTSIDE ENDOCRINOLOGY — FOLLOW-UP
Visit: 02/10/2026   cc: PCP

Macroprolactinoma, on cabergoline 0.25 mg twice weekly since late November. Taking it reliably at bedtime, tolerating it. Breast leakage is less than before but still there. No menses yet. Vision about the same to her; no headaches.

Exam: temporal field restriction on confrontation, right more than left, unchanged from November.

Prolactin 2/3: 140 ng/mL (250 before treatment). Moving the right way but well above normal.

Plan: increase cabergoline to 0.5 mg twice weekly, one full tablet. Repeat MRI this summer, timed with a prolactin. Sooner for headaches or vision change.

— Endocrinology

documents.title: Annual Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Yearly physical. Turns 31 in September.

Interval: pituitary macroprolactinoma diagnosed in November, followed by endocrinology. On cabergoline 0.5 mg twice weekly since February. Prolactin 250 at diagnosis, 140 in February per the endo letter. Still no periods. Still has some milky leakage from both breasts, less than last fall. The last few months she has had a dull headache now and then, usually late in the day; she put it down to grading and screens. Side vision feels no worse to her. Endo plans a repeat MRI and prolactin this summer; the appointment is in July.

ROS otherwise negative. Sleeping fine, mood good, PHQ-9 is 2.

Meds: cabergoline 0.5 mg PO twice weekly. NKDA.
SH: still teaching, never smoker, wine once or twice a week.

Exam: vitals as charted, BMI normal. Comfortable. Thyroid smooth, no nodules. Heart S1 S2 regular, no murmur. Lungs without wheeze or crackle. Abdomen soft, nontender. Pelvic: normal external genitalia, cervix without lesion, Pap with HPV collected. Breasts not re-examined, discharge as described. Neuro: cranial nerves intact apart from her known temporal field loss, which I did not formally retest; strength and gait normal.

A/P
1. Prolactinoma on cabergoline, prolactin still high in February. New intermittent dull headaches are worth telling endocrinology about before July; I'll send them a note. If headaches become frequent or severe, or vision worsens, she should not wait for July and should be seen urgently.
2. Health maintenance: Pap with HPV today. Flu and COVID vaccines this coming October. Tdap status unknown in the old records; will look again next year.
Next physical in a year.

Asked whether they want the MRI sooner than July. Office acknowledged receipt; will leave timing to them.

reports.study: MRI brain with and without contrast
reports.text:
EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT IMAGING
Exam: MRI brain without and with gadolinium, including thin coronal and sagittal sequences of the sella.
Indication: known pituitary adenoma, headaches, worsening peripheral vision.
Comparison: outside MRI 11/06/2025, report available.

Findings: Sellar mass measuring 1.3 cm in greatest craniocaudal dimension on coronal post-contrast images, previously reported as 1.5 cm. The suprasellar component elevates and compresses the optic chiasm. No intratumoral hemorrhage or infarct to suggest apoplexy. Cavernous sinuses without invasion. No hydrocephalus. Remainder of the brain normal. No acute intracranial abnormality.
reports.conclusion: 1.3 cm pituitary macroadenoma, smaller than the prior report, still compressing the optic chiasm. No hemorrhage.

documents.title: Emergency Department Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
REGIONAL EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT — PHYSICIAN RECORD
Arrived 6/30/2026 18:40. Received by the primary care office 7/2/2026.

CC: headaches, vision getting worse.

HPI: 30F with a pituitary prolactinoma diagnosed last November, on cabergoline through endocrinology. For several months she has had recurring dull headaches, now most days, and over the same period her peripheral vision has been slipping; today the headache would not settle and she came in. She continues to have spontaneous milky discharge from both nipples; not pregnant, not breastfeeding. No sudden thunderclap onset, no vomiting, no double vision, no fever.

Meds: cabergoline 0.5 mg twice weekly. Allergies: NKDA.
PMH/PSH: prolactinoma; tonsillectomy as a child.
Family: hypothyroid mother, hypertensive father; no pituitary or endocrine tumors.
Social: math teacher, never smoked, light wine use.

Exam: vitals in flowsheet, afebrile. Alert, oriented, uncomfortable but not toxic. Pupils equal and reactive, fundi without papilledema. Confrontation fields show peripheral loss in both eyes. Remaining cranial nerves, strength, sensation, coordination and gait normal. Bilateral galactorrhea on exam. Neck supple.

Results: prolactin 131 ng/mL (ref 4-23), markedly elevated. Urine hCG negative. BMP and CBC unremarkable. MRI brain: 1.3 cm sellar mass compressing the optic chiasm, no hemorrhage.

MDM: known macroprolactinoma with chiasmal compression and persistent symptoms on cabergoline. No apoplexy, no hydrocephalus, neuro otherwise intact. Does not require admission. Spoke with on-call endocrinology, who will see her within two weeks.

Disposition: discharged home, stable, 23:55. Return for sudden severe headache, rapid vision loss, vomiting or confusion. Continue cabergoline until seen by endocrinology. Copy to PCP and endocrinology.

documents.title: Went to the ER last night

documents.body: Wanted you to know I ended up in the ER last night. The headaches got more frequent and my side vision is worse. They did an MRI, the tumor is a little smaller but still pressing on the optic nerves. They called endocrinology and I'm supposed to be seen in the next couple of weeks. Sent home. Just wanted you to have the update.

documents.title: RE: Went to the ER last night
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Thank you for letting me know, and I'm sorry you had a rough night. Good that the scan showed no bleeding and that it is a bit smaller. We'll get the ER record. Keep the endocrinology visit, and if the headache becomes sudden and severe or your vision drops quickly, go back in. I'm here if you want to talk it through before then.

documents.title: Endocrinology Follow-up
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
OUTSIDE ENDOCRINOLOGY — FOLLOW-UP AFTER ED VISIT
Visit: 07/14/2026   cc: PCP

Seen in the ED 6/30 for headaches and worsening peripheral vision. MRI there: adenoma now 1.3 cm, down from 1.5 cm, but still compressing the chiasm. Prolactin 131 ng/mL on cabergoline 0.5 mg twice weekly (250 at baseline, 140 in February). Headaches continue several days a week. Galactorrhea persists. Amenorrhea continues.

Exam: bitemporal field restriction on confrontation, right worse.

Assessment: macroprolactinoma with incomplete biochemical and radiographic response to cabergoline and persistent chiasmal compression with visual symptoms.

Plan:
- Increase cabergoline to 1 mg (two 0.5 mg tablets) twice weekly.
- Formal visual field testing with ophthalmology, ordered.
- Referral to neurosurgery for an opinion on transsphenoidal surgery, given the chiasm.
- Prolactin in 4 to 6 weeks.

— Endocrinology

documents.title: Neurosurgery Consultation
documents.author: neurosurgery
documents.body:
OUTSIDE NEUROSURGERY — NEW PATIENT CONSULTATION
Visit: 08/11/2026
Referred by endocrinology; copy to PCP.

30-year-old teacher with a prolactin-secreting pituitary macroadenoma diagnosed 11/2025. Cabergoline has lowered prolactin from 250 to 131 ng/mL and reduced the tumor from 1.5 to 1.3 cm, but the June MRI shows continued compression of the optic chiasm and she reports ongoing headaches and peripheral vision loss. Cabergoline was recently raised to 1 mg twice weekly by endocrinology.

Exam: alert, fluent. Bitemporal field deficit to confrontation. Otherwise nonfocal.

Imaging reviewed personally: 1.3 cm sellar and suprasellar adenoma elevating the chiasm, no cavernous sinus invasion, favorable sphenoid anatomy.

Discussion: with symptomatic chiasmal compression despite medical therapy, I recommend endoscopic endonasal transsphenoidal resection. We reviewed goals (decompress the chiasm, debulk or remove the tumor), the expected hospital stay, and risks including CSF leak, sodium and water balance problems, pituitary hormone deficiency, bleeding, infection and, rarely, vision worsening. She would like time to think it over and to see the formal visual field results before deciding. She will continue cabergoline in the meantime.

Plan: return visit once fields are done to make a decision.

— Neurosurgery
